units.title: Hello, D
units.summary: Write your first D program: import std.stdio, start in main and print text and numbers with writeln and write.

lesson.md: A D program is a text file that ends in `.d`. A compiler such as `dmd` or `ldc2` turns it into a program that you can run. Here is the classic first program. It prints one line of text.

Let us read it line by line. `import std.stdio;` loads the module for input and output (`stdio` means standard input and output) from Phobos, the standard library of D. `void main()` is the function where every program starts. `void` means that it gives back no value. The braces `{` and `}` hold the code of the function.
`writeln` writes text to the screen and then ends the line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, world!"`, is called a **string**. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.

You can give `writeln` several values, separated by commas. It prints them one after another, **without** spaces between them. Numbers need no quotes, and D calculates `2 + 3` before it prints. Text in quotes is printed exactly as it is.
`write` prints like `writeln`, but it does not end the line. The next output continues on the same line. `writeln()` with nothing inside only ends the line.
A **comment** starts with `//` and goes to the end of the line. The compiler ignores it. In this course, comments only show results. `*` multiplies and `-` subtracts.
Inside a string, `\n` starts a new line and `\"` prints a double quote. These pairs are called escape sequences.
D is case-sensitive: `writeln` works, but `Writeln` or `WRITELN` is an error. A missing semicolon is also an error, and the compiler tells you the line.

card: `void main() { }` is where the program starts
`// comment` is ignored, `;` ends a statement

exercises.explain: `writeln` comes from `std.stdio`. `print` and `echo` do not exist in D, and `System.out.println` is Java.

exercises.explain: `writeln` prints its values one after another without spaces. It does not add them.

exercises.statement: Every D program starts running in the function `main`.
exercises.explain: `void main()` is the starting point. A program without `main` cannot be built.

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables with the types int, double, string and bool, and let auto and immutable help you.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. In D you write the type first, then the name, then `=` and the value. `int` holds whole numbers, `double` holds decimal numbers, `string` holds text and `bool` holds `true` or `false`.

You give a variable a new value with `=`. `score += 2` is short for `score = score + 2`. `-=`, `*=` and `/=` work the same way. The type of a variable never changes: putting a string into an `int` variable is an error.

D calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, and `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`. When you divide two `int` values, the result is an `int` and the rest is dropped. `%` gives the rest of a division. If one of the numbers is a `double`, like `7.0`, the result is a `double`.
With `auto` instead of a type, the compiler picks the type from the value. `typeof(x).stringof` gives the name of the type of `x` as text, so you can check it.

A variable marked `immutable` can never change after it gets its value. Use it for values that must stay fixed. Like `auto`, `immutable` can pick the type by itself: `immutable weeks = 3;` is an `int`.
If you try to change an `immutable` variable, for example with `days = 8;`, the program does not compile.

A variable without a value gets a default value: `0` for `int`, `false` for `bool` and an empty text for `string`. A `double` starts as `nan`, which means "not a number". It reminds you that you forgot to set a value.

card: `auto x = 3.5;` the compiler picks the type

exercises.explain: `b` gets `10` when it is created. Changing `a` later does not change `b`, so `1 + 10` is `11`.
17 divided by 5 is 3 with a rest of 2. With two `int` values, `/` gives `3` and `%` gives `2`.

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Join strings with ~, read characters and slices, use std.string functions and format output with writefln.

lesson.md: In D you join two strings with `~` (the tilde), not with `+`. `s ~= "!"` adds text to the end of `s`.

`s.length` gives the number of characters. `s[0]` is the first character, because counting starts at `0`. `s[1 .. 4]` is a **slice**: the characters from position 1 up to, but not including, position 4. Inside the brackets, `$` means the length, so `s[$ - 1]` is the last character.

The module `std.string` has many useful functions. `strip` removes spaces at the start and the end, `toUpper` and `toLower` change the case, `indexOf` gives the position of a text (or `-1` if it is not there) and `replace` swaps one text for another. You call them with a dot after the string: `s.toUpper()`.

lesson.output:
Hello, D
HELLO, D
hello, d
7
Bye, D

lesson.md: `"a" + "b"` does not compile, because `+` is only for numbers. `~` only joins strings, so `"Age: " ~ age` with an `int` variable `age` does not compile either.
To turn a number into a string, use `to!string(n)` from the module `std.conv`. `to!int("42")` goes the other way. The `!` gives `to` the type you want to get.

`writefln` prints a format string and ends the line. Each placeholder is replaced by the next value: `%s` fits any value, `%d` a whole number and `%.2f` a decimal number with two digits after the point. `format` from `std.string` works the same way but gives back the string instead of printing it.

lesson.output:
Ana is 30 years old.
Height: 1.68 m
Ana/30

exercises.explain: `banana` has 6 characters, and `s[1]` is the second one, `a`. `writeln` prints both without a space.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with if, else, the ?: operator and switch.

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses `( )`, the code in braces. `else if` checks another condition, and `else` runs when no condition was `true`. You compare values with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.
You combine conditions with `&&` (and: both must be `true`), `||` (or: at least one must be `true`) and `!` (not: turns `true` into `false` and back).
The operator `? :` picks one of two values: `cond ? a : b` gives `a` when `cond` is `true` and `b` otherwise. Here `n % 2 == 0` checks if `n` is even.
`=` gives a value, `==` compares. If you write `if (x = 5)` by mistake, D stops with an error instead of running wrong code.

`switch` compares one value with several `case` labels and runs the matching one. A case can list several values, separated by commas. Each case ends with `break`. D does not let a case run into the next one: forgetting `break` is an error. `default` runs when no case matches, and D requires it.
`switch` also works with strings.
`case 80: .. case 89:` matches every value from 80 to 89, both ends included.

exercises.explain: 15 is not at least 20, but it is at least 10, so the `else if` branch runs.
`a > 5` is `false`, but `b > 5` is `true`. With `||` one `true` side is enough.
`3` is listed in `case 2, 3:`, so that case runs and `break` ends the `switch`.
The first case has no `break`, so it would run into the next case. D does not allow this and stops with an error.
`x = 4` is an assignment, not a comparison. D does not accept it as a condition. Write `x == 4`.

exercises.code: writeln(!(5 > 3));
exercises.explain: `5 > 3` is `true`, and `!` turns it into `false`.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for, foreach over ranges like 0 .. 5, while and do-while, and control loops with break and continue.

lesson.md: A `for` loop has three parts in its parentheses, separated by semicolons: a start (`int i = 1`), a condition that is checked before each round (`i <= 3`) and a step that runs after each round. `i++` adds 1 to `i`, and `i--` subtracts 1.
`foreach (i; 0 .. 3)` is the easiest way to count. `0 .. 3` is a **range**: the numbers from 0 up to 3, **without** 3. The loop runs once for each number, and `i` holds the current one.
`foreach` also walks over the characters of a string, one after another. `foreach_reverse` walks backwards.
`while` repeats its code as long as the condition is `true`. Make sure something inside the loop changes, or the loop never ends.
`do { } while (cond);` checks the condition **after** each round, so the code runs at least once.
`continue` jumps straight to the next round, and `break` ends the loop at once.

card: `break` ends the loop, `continue` goes to the next round

`n` becomes 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. After 5 rounds `n < 20` is `false`.

`0 .. 3` gives 0, 1 and 2, so the code runs 3 times.
A `do`-`while` loop runs once before it checks the condition. `6 < 3` is `false`, so it stops after one round.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with parameters and return values, change variables with ref and chain calls with UFCS.

lesson.md: A **function** is a named block of code that you can call again and again. You write the return type, the name and the parameters in parentheses, each with its type. `return` gives a value back to the caller. A `void` function gives nothing back. Functions are written outside of `main`.
In D, a function can come before or after `main`. A parameter can have a default value with `=`. If you leave it out in the call, the default is used.
A function can have several `return` statements. The first one that runs ends the function at once.
If the return type is not `void`, every way through the function must end with `return` and a value. Otherwise the program does not compile.
Normally a function gets a **copy** of each value. If it changes the copy, the caller's variable stays the same. With `ref` before the parameter, the function works on the caller's variable itself.

D has **UFCS** (Uniform Function Call Syntax): you can write `f(x)` as `x.f()`, and `f(x, y)` as `x.f(y)`. When there is nothing left in the parentheses, you can drop them: `x.f`. This is why `s.toUpper()` from the strings unit works. Chains read from left to right.
Use UFCS when it makes the order of steps easier to read: `3.plus(2).square` first adds, then squares.

card: `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`
`int f(int x, int y = 10)` has a default value
`ref int n` changes the caller's variable
UFCS: `f(x, y)` is the same as `x.f(y)`

exercises.explain: The inner call gives `6`, and the outer call doubles it to `12`.
With `ref`, `a` is the variable `v` itself, so `v` becomes `10`.
With UFCS, `10.sub(4)` is the same as `sub(10, 4)`, which is `6`.
Without `ref`, `bump` changes only its own copy. `x` in `main` stays `3`.

exercises.explain: With UFCS the first argument goes before the dot: `add(5, 2)` becomes `5.add(2)`.

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Keep many values in dynamic arrays, append with ~=, cut slices and look up values by key in associative arrays.

lesson.md: An **array** holds several values of the same type in a fixed order. `int[]` is an array of `int` values. You write the values in square brackets. `a[0]` is the first element, `a.length` the number of elements, and `writeln` can print the whole array.
These arrays are **dynamic**: they can grow. `~=` adds an element (or another array) at the end, and `~` joins two arrays into a new one.
`foreach` walks over all elements. With two names, like `foreach (i, name; names)`, you also get the position.

lesson.output:
Ana
Ben
Cleo
0: Ana
1: Ben
2: Cleo

lesson.md: `a[1 .. 4]` is a slice, as with strings, and `$` is the length. A slice does not copy the elements: it **shares** them with the array, so a change through the slice changes the array too. The same is true for `b = a`. `.dup` makes a real copy.
An index outside the array, like `nums[5]` for an array with 5 elements, stops the program with an error. The last valid index is `nums.length - 1`.

An **associative array** stores values under keys. `int[string] ages` has `string` keys and `int` values: the value type comes first, the key type goes in the brackets. `ages["Ana"] = 30` adds or changes a value. `"Ben" in ages` checks if a key exists, and `remove` deletes one.
Reading a key that does not exist stops the program with an error. `ages.get("Zoe", 0)` gives `0` instead. The order of the keys is not fixed, so do not rely on it.

exercises.explain: `a[1]` is `8` and `a[$ - 1]` is the last element, `16`. 8 + 16 is 24.
Two elements are added to the two at the start: `[1, 2, 3, 1]` has 4 elements.
The slice takes positions 2 and 3, which hold `7` and `8`. Position 4 is not included.
`b = a` does not copy the elements. Both names share them, so the change through `b` is visible in `a`.

units.title: Structs and classes
units.summary: Build your own types: structs with fields and methods, and classes with constructors, new and inheritance.

lesson.md: A `struct` groups related values under one name and so creates a new type. The values inside are called **fields**. `Point(3, 4)` creates a `Point` and fills the fields in order. You reach a field with a dot: `p.x`.
A function inside a struct is called a **method**. It can use the fields directly. You call it with a dot, like `r.area()`. As with UFCS, you can leave out empty parentheses.
Structs are **values**: `b = a` copies all fields, so changing `b` leaves `a` as it was. A field can have a default value, like `int count = 0;`.

A `class` also has fields and methods, but you create objects with `new`. A class variable is a **reference**: after `b = a`, both names point to the same object. The method `this(...)` is the **constructor**; `new` calls it. Inside, `this.owner` means the field, while `owner` alone is the parameter.

A class can build on another class: `class Dog : Animal` gets all fields and methods of `Animal`. `super(name)` calls the constructor of `Animal`, and `override` replaces a method. A `Dog` object can be stored in an `Animal` variable and still uses its own method.
A class variable without `new` is `null`: it points to no object. Calling a method on it crashes the program.
Use a `struct` for small values like points or dates. Use a `class` when several parts of the program must share one object, or when you need inheritance.

card: `struct P { int x; int y; }` and `P(1, 2)`
methods are functions inside a struct or class
structs are copied, class objects are shared

`writeln` prints a struct as its name followed by the field values in parentheses.
The method uses the field `c`: 100 * 9 / 5 + 32 is 212.
